51322d004c17054c: Dalam dunia politik moden yang penuh dengan kebanjiran maklumat, propaganda tidak lagi beroperasi dengan cara lama yang kasar, memaksa dan terang-terangan. Propaganda hari ini bergerak melalui bahasa, khususnya bahasa yang samar, berlapik, dan mengelirukan.

Menurut Jason Stanley, Profesor Falsafah di Yale University dan penulis buku How Propaganda Works (2015), propaganda moden berjaya bukan kerana ia mengelirukan, tetapi kerana ia menggunakan kebenaran yang difahamkan secara keliru. Bahasa propaganda menjadi alat untuk mengawal fikiran rakyat dengan cara yang lembut, hampir tidak dapat dikesan, namun sangat efektif dalam membentuk apa yang rakyat fikir benar.

Stanley menjelaskan propaganda moden berfungsi dengan cara menghalang wacana kritikal. Ia bukan sekadar menutup akses kepada maklumat, tetapi memanipulasi makna maklumat tersebut sehingga rakyat tidak dapat membuat penilaian rasional.

Bahasa yang digunakan kelihatan profesional, teknikal dan dilihat rasional namun sebenarnya ia menyembunyikan tindakan sebenar atau menutup kegagalan. Contoh mudah: apabila subsidi ditarik balik, ia akan disebut sebagai ‘penstrukturan semula mekanisme bantuan’ atau ‘rasionalisasi subsidi’. Apabila berlaku masalah dalam pentadbiran, kita mendengar frasa ‘isu dalam perhatian’, ‘penilaian sedang dibuat’, atau ‘perkara ini sedang dikaji secara menyeluruh’. Semua ayat ini nampak sopan dan meyakinkan, tetapi jika diteliti secara mendalam, ia tidak menjelaskan apa-apa pun.

Seni propaganda melalui bahasa samar ini berfungsi kerana ia memenuhi dua keperluan politik: pertama, menjaga imej pemerintah; kedua, menenangkan rakyat supaya tidak panik. Stanley membahagikan propaganda kepada dua kategori.
Supporting propaganda menggunakan bahasa yang kelihatan menyokong nilai demokrasi seperti ketelusan, profesionalisme dan kestabilan, tetapi tujuan sebenarnya ialah mengekalkan kuasa pemerintah.

Undermining propaganda pula ialah bahasa yang kelihatan rasional tetapi digunakan untuk menutup ketidakjujuran atau tindakan yang bertentangan dengan kepentingan awam. Kedua-duanya menggunakan bahasa yang sama iaitu kabur, berlapik, dan sabar berfungsi dalam konteks yang berbeza.

Dalam masyarakat moden, bahasa berlapik digunakan untuk mengurus persepsi dan emosi rakyat. Apabila isu sensitif timbul seperti kenaikan harga barang, kegagalan projek mega, kelemahan institusi, atau ketegangan kaum, pemerintah cenderung memilih frasa-frasa yang menenangkan. ‘Mengawal tekanan ekonomi global’, ‘menyelaraskan semula struktur fiskal’, ‘memperkukuh ekosistem pentadbiran’, atau ‘melakukan penambahbaikan proses’. Semuanya adalah contoh bagaimana bahasa digunakan untuk melunakkan realiti. Rakyat mendengar perkataan yang sedap, tetapi tidak memahami apakah tindakan sebenar yang sedang dilakukan.

Stanley menegaskan propaganda moden juga bekerja melalui kebanjiran maklumat. Dalam sistem di mana media dikawal secara langsung atau tidak langsung, maklumat satu sisi menjadi norma. Rakyat bergantung kepada ‘kebenaran rasmi’, dan bahasa pemerintah menjadi bahasa media.

Maka. gaya bahasa berlapik yang sama diulang melalui berita, kenyataan akhbar, laporan ekonomi dan ucapan pemimpin. Ulangan ini akhirnya menjadikan bahasa propaganda sebagai bahasa biasa. Rakyat tidak menyedari mereka sedang dipengaruhi, kerana bahasa yang digunakan bukan bahasa kasar atau menipu, tetapi bahasa yang nampak profesional.

Bahasa samar juga digunakan untuk mencipta musuh yang tidak bernama. Teknik ini sangat berkesan kerana ia menanam emosi tanpa perlu membuktikan apa-apa. Ungkapan seperti ‘pihak tertentu sedang cuba menggugat kestabilan negara’, ‘agenda asing sedang menyusup’, atau ‘unsur ekstrem tidak boleh dipandang ringan’ sering digunakan tanpa identiti jelas.

Rakyat mendengar ancaman, merasai kebimbangan, tetapi tidak mengetahui siapa musuh sebenar. Inilah teknik propaganda yang menanam rasa takut secara terkawal dan sekali gus memberikan justifikasi kepada tindakan pemerintah untuk bertindak keras, menggubal undang-undang tambahan atau mengawal ruang awam.

Dalam konteks Malaysia, budaya bahasa berlapik sudah lama berakar. Ketika isu perkauman timbul, istilah ‘sensitiviti masyarakat’ digunakan untuk mengelakkan perbincangan terus tentang diskriminasi atau ketidaksamarataan.

Ketika berlaku skandal, istilah ‘ketirisan kecil’ digunakan. Ketika ekonomi merosot, istilah ‘penyesuaian struktur ekonomi’ menjadi pilihan. Apabila kerajaan gagal mengurus bencana, ungkapan ‘cabaran penyelarasan’ digunakan bagi mengalihkan perhatian daripada kelemahan pengurusan. Bahasa ini tidak salah, tetapi ia menjarakkan rakyat daripada memahami realiti sebenar.

Propaganda melalui bahasa samar bekerja bukan dengan cara memaksa rakyat percaya sesuatu, tetapi dengan cara mengisi ruang antara penjelasan dan kekeliruan. Rakyat yang tidak mendapat maklumat sebenar akhirnya membina naratif sendiri berdasarkan andaian dan perasaan.

Inilah yang dimaksudkan Stanley apabila beliau mengatakan propaganda moden adakalanya memanipulasi rasional manusia. Ia mengehadkan rakyat untuk berfikir, tetapi mendidik mereka menerima kabus sebagai kebenaran.

Dalam era digital, bahasa samar menjadi lebih penting kerana maklumat tersebar dengan pantas. Propagandis perlu mengurus persepsi dengan cepat, dan bahasa berlapik memberikan mereka masa. Satu kenyataan kabur sudah cukup untuk menghentikan kritikan selama 24 jam, sementara strategi komunikasi seterusnya disusun. Contohnya, ketika berlaku masalah dalam sesuatu operasi kenyataan seperti ‘sistem sedang dipertingkatkan’ atau ‘masalah teknikal sedang diselesaikan’ membantu menutup tekanan awam sementara ruang masa dicari boleh menyelesaikan masalah.

Kesannya, rakyat berdepan dunia yang penuh dengan ayat tetapi kosong makna. Mereka mendengar banyak perkataan, tetapi sedikit fakta. Mereka rasa diberi maklumat, tetapi sebenarnya menerima secara samar. Propaganda paling berjaya ialah propaganda yang menjadikan rakyat percaya mereka memahami sesuatu isu padahal mereka tidak diberi maklumat sebenar.

Jason Stanley merumuskan hal ini dengan tepat iaitu: ‘Propaganda ialah manipulasi kehendak rasional manusia sehingga perbincangan terhenti’. Inilah kekuatan gaya bahasa samar dan berlapik. Ia bukan hanya menutup kebenaran, tetapi menutup pintu untuk bertanya.
Dan selama pintu itu tertutup, propaganda menguasai seluruh ruang pemikiran masyarakat.

c6e7cabff185da96: An extract from Plato's "Republic" reads: "Said the old Cephalus to the younger Socrates, 'Older men of my age flock together and in our meeting my common tale is – I cannot eat, I cannot drink, the pleasure of youth and love have fled away, there was a good time once, but now gone, and life is no longer ours.'"
Such is the reality of ageing, and perhaps there is a lesson here for politicians who have overstayed their welcome in the political arena.
I hope that the impending Melaka state election will be an eye-opener for Malaysians, particularly our political leaders who seem to have difficulty recognising when it is time to call it a day.
PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang and many politicians of his generation should seriously consider retiring from politics.
Judging from their regular outbursts and political pronouncements, some appear increasingly disconnected from the realities, aspirations and concerns of ordinary Malaysians.
Their political vocabulary, arguments and preoccupations seem to belong to another era.
Hadi's latest outburst is a case in point.
In his reaction to the confidence and supply agreement (CSA) between opposition MPs and the government, he likened the arrangement to the deception of the Dajjal.

Whatever one's views about the CSA, surely there are more constructive ways to debate a parliamentary arrangement. It is one thing to disagree with a political agreement; it is quite another to invoke apocalyptic religious imagery to discredit it.
Such rhetoric does little to advance public understanding or the quality of our political discourse.
Malaysia is rapidly changing
This is precisely the problem with some of our ageing political leaders. They seem more interested in fighting yesterday's political battles than addressing tomorrow's challenges.
Our younger population is concerned about employment, housing affordability, wages, education, technology, artificial intelligence, green agenda and the rising cost of living.
They want practical solutions, economic opportunities and a government that understands the world they are growing up in.
Yet much of our political conversation remains trapped in old rivalries, identity politics, religious arguments and endless disputes over who should be in power and who should become prime minister.
How much longer must Malaysians listen to identity and religious politics from the same personalities with the same political arguments?

Hadi is not alone. Former prime minister Muhyiddin Yassin, deputy prime minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, former federal minister Rais Yatim and several other long-serving political figures should seriously consider leaving the political arena as well.

They have had their opportunities, occupied important positions and exercised considerable influence over the country's political upheavals. They should recognise that political leadership is not a lifetime entitlement.

There is a difference between serving the country and holding on to political power. After decades in politics, surely there comes a time when personal ambition must give way to institutional renewal.

Our political parties should not be personal properties, nor should their leadership positions become permanent appointments. No individual should be indispensable to a political party, let alone to an entire nation.
Malaysia's political weakness

One of Malaysia's biggest political weaknesses is the reluctance of senior politicians to groom and give way to younger leaders. They continue to dominate party structures, determine candidate selections and control political narratives.
Young politicians are often expected to wait patiently for their turn, while the same senior personalities continue to occupy the top positions election after election.
This is unhealthy.
A political party cannot produce new leaders or renew its leadership in a hierarchy that is dominated by ageing politicians. PAS, Bersatu and Umno are clear examples.
Do they genuinely believe in the future of their parties or are they simply protecting their own positions?
I fully agree with the argument about giving younger politicians greater opportunities.

The emergence of younger leaders should not merely be an electoral gimmick to attract younger voters. They must be given real responsibilities, decision-making authority and opportunities to shape national policies.
Of course, being young does not automatically make someone a capable leader. Experience, integrity, competence and sound judgment matter.

But these qualities cannot be the exclusive possessions of older politicians, either. Young leaders need opportunities to acquire experience, and they cannot do so if the older generation refuses to release its grip.

Let the younger generation make mistakes, learn from them and develop their own leadership capabilities. That is how political maturity is built. We cannot keep telling young people that they lack experience while denying them the opportunity to gain it.

There is also a larger democratic question. How can we expect a country to embrace new ideas, modernise its institutions and prepare for the future when much of its political leadership remains occupied by personalities whose political careers began several decades ago?
The world is moving on
Technology, economic structures, international competition and the expectations of younger citizens are changing. Political leadership must change with them.
For Hadi, Muhyiddin, Zahid and scores of others who have spent much of their lives in politics, perhaps the greatest contribution they can now make is to step aside gracefully.

They can offer advice, share their experience and allow the next generation to take responsibility. They do not need to remain party presidents, political kingmakers or permanent fixtures in our national politics.

The Melaka election should be more than another contest between political coalitions. It should also be an opportunity for voters to consider the kind of leadership they want for the next decade and beyond.

Malaysia needs a political generation that looks forward, not backwards; one that debates policies rather than personalities, solves problems rather than manufactures controversies, and builds institutions rather than protects individual political careers.
Enough is enough. You have had your time. You have had your opportunities. It is time to let go.

3b237e183dd5187e: Malaysians have come to take our festivals for granted, gliding through Deepavali as if it were just another ordinary day on the calendar—a polite pause amid the roar of traffic and the clatter of daily life.

Yet, if we close our eyes for a moment and picture it—houses alive with oil lamps glowing in every direction, the air fragrant with sesame-scented murukku, and the laughter of children in new clothes spilling onto the streets—we are reminded of the festival's vibrant soul.
What few of us realise, however, is that this radiant celebration once rose in daring rebellion.
Today, Deepavali burns brightly as a public holiday across Peninsular Malaysia, with Sabah having quietly folded it into its own calendar of observances.

But few know the breathless, dramatic saga of how this festival was once locked in a fierce, cinematic battle for supremacy—not merely over lamps and sweets, but for the very right to be recognised as a national holiday.
That epic contest was fought not against external forces, but between two towering pillars of the Hindu community itself: Deepavali and Thaipusam.

Both claimed the same prize: a full public holiday so their celebrations could soar to their unbridled heights. One side believed Deepavali, with its blaze of lights that welcomed every soul under the sun, was the broader, more inclusive flame that would carry Indian identity into the future. The other saw in Thaipusam—with its profound message of inner victory through devotion and discipline—the sacred, undying fire that needed to be nurtured.
The battle was real, heated, and decided in colonial Singapore in 1914—a moment that still echoes today, though almost all of us remain blissfully unaware of it.
I wonder how many Malaysians—Indians among them—know that the first Indian-related public holiday in British Malaya was actually for Thaipusam?

Then spelled Tai-pusum, it first flickered into existence in the 1879 Holidays Ordinance IX as a bank holiday in Penang. In British Malaya, bank holidays existed primarily to ensure the colony's commercial engine paused simultaneously.

Thaipusam secured its spot because of a dynamic Indian merchant class in Penang and because government departments, most notably the Public Works Department and the municipal council, were overwhelmingly staffed by Indians.

Then came 1914. The colonial administration decided that one set of uniform public holidays should cover the entire Straits Settlements. Operating under the rule of "one major festival of each of the main races," a Bill was drafted nominating Thaipusam for the Indian community as it was already a holiday in Penang.

Here the story takes a twist. The English-speaking elites and merchants of Singapore preferred Deepavali. Their community was a diverse tapestry woven from Telugus, Gujaratis, Sindhis, Malayalees, and Punjabis—not just Tamils. Thaipusam, they argued, was too narrow, too tied to the Chettiar community, and too purely religious for their cosmopolitan vision.
Led by the formidable Dr N Veerasamy Naidu—one of Singapore’s first Indian doctors and a municipal commissioner—the merchant group petitioned Governor Sir Arthur Henderson Young.

Their letter glowed with eloquence and loyalty, speaking of making Deepavali “an act of grace which will be greatly appreciated not only by the 60 or 70,000 most loyal and submissive subjects of His most gracious Majesty the Emperor of India but by the future generations of the permanent residents of the colony”.
They reminded the governor that Deepavali was already observed as a public holiday in India and that it was a public holiday in Singapore in the year 1912.

The movement quickly gained momentum. In February 1914, roughly a thousand prominent Hindus packed the Hindu Association on Belilios Road. Veerasamy, who chaired the meeting, reminded those present that Deepavali had been declared a holiday in Singapore in 1912, thanks to an earlier petition through the Hindu and Muhammadan Endowments Board. Yet a similar application in 1913 had not succeeded.
Now the stakes were higher — the holiday would cover the whole colony. And it would not require annual petitions.

Among those present were influential merchants and elites such as MV Pillay, SMR Naidu, KN Kothary, Nagar Das, Chotiirmal, M Soomapah, Mungul Singh, Dr Bardhan, Veer Singh, Thambyrajah, Veeraragava Aiyar, Singaram Pillai and Sivakadacha Padayachi.

Leaders like MV Pillay argued passionately that Deepavali suited Singapore’s multi-racial fabric better, allowing other races to share in its social joy, whereas Thaipusam remained a strictly intense, specialised Hindu observance.

Noting that Deepavali was a public holiday in India, Pillay insisted the same should apply in the Straits Settlements of Singapore, Penang and Malacca (now Melaka). He added that Indian workers in the PWD and municipal council in Singapore were usually given a holiday on Deepavali day and not Thaipusam day.

The meeting adopted a proposal to send a delegation to convince Governor Young to make Deepavali the public holiday for Hindus in the colony. MV Pillay, who moved the motion, claimed that it was the Chettiar community that was pushing for Thaipusam, and that in doing so it had disregarded the wishes of other communities.

Not everyone agreed with this resolution. Some Singapore Hindus, including those not from the Chettiar community, wrote directly to the governor insisting the original Bill remain unchanged. They claimed that Veerasamy’s group did not speak for everyone and that the government would earn the deep gratitude of the community by following Penang's example.

A fierce but polite battle ensued between supporters of both festivals. Ultimately, the British authorities chose to listen to the Singapore merchant class and the more influential English-speaking elites.
They dropped Thaipusam from the Bill and substituted it with Deepavali, passing the Holidays (Amendment) Ordinance 1914 for the entire colony of Singapore, Penang, and Malacca.

I was unable to find any record that showed strong protests from Penang and Malacca Hindus. I suspect the Chettiars - a small, self-reliant and self-effacing mercantile community that prefers to conduct its business in quiet dignity - decided that Thaipusam would still be observed with due respect even if it was no longer an official holiday.

But the ripple effect soon reached the Federated Malay States (FMS). By April 1915, KT Parmanan Pillay, president of the Sri Mahamariamman Temple on High Street (Jalan Tun HS Lee), wrote to Selangor Resident Edward George Broadrick, telling him that the local Hindu community had passed a resolution asking for both Thaipusam and Deepavali to be declared public holidays.

In Taiping, then the capital of Perak, a public meeting was held in the town hall on Feb 21, 1926 under the chairmanship of H Rethinasamy Pillai, reportedly attended by Indians from several parts of the FMS. The meeting resolved to urge the British authorities to also make Deepavali a public holiday in the FMS, as there was then none for the community.

One of the leaders, V Murugasu Pillai, in a letter to the chief secretary to the FMS government Sir William George Maxwell, noted that Deepavali was already a holiday in the neighbouring Straits Settlements. He claimed that the views of the “Indian and Ceylonese communities” in Selangor, Negri Sembilan and Pahang had also been obtained and that all of them were unanimous in voicing the request for a holiday for Deepavali.

Whether the colonial authorities fully capitulated back then remains slightly murky in the archives, but the framework of history eventually birthed the national holiday we enjoy today under the 1951 Holidays Act.
Today, Deepavali’s lights burn brightly across Malaysia, while in several states, Thaipusam remains a powerful public holiday observed with equal vitality.

Ultimately, the story of Deepavali’s rise is one of quiet endurance rather than conquest. Two great flames once stood at opposite ends of the Hindu night sky—one broad and welcoming, the other focused and sacred. Colonial hands chose one over the other a century ago, but time has proven that neither had to be extinguished.

Today, both Deepavali and Thaipusam light up the Malaysian landscape side by side, proving that traditions fought for with such passion never truly fade. They simply learn to glow together, year after year, across the same land.
Happy Deepavali.

73621b4b798e434c: PARIS, Nov 8 — “Correction” is not the word investors want to hear, but the stampede out of AI and technology stocks this week has heightened doubts about the sustainability of the four-year bull run for markets.
Further declines would have wide-ranging financial and economic consequences amid the massive AI spending, much of it fuelled by companies taking on huge amounts of debt.
AFP takes a look at how tech sector weakness could impact governments and households.
The AI motor
Outlays on data centres to train and power artificial intelligence models have become one of the main growth engines for the US economy, the world’s largest.
“That contributed to 30 per cent of growth in the United States in 2025 and 2026,” said Bruno Cavalier, economist at the bank Oddo BHF, with spending on data centres surging by 150 per cent.
The resulting demand for cutting-edge chips and other high-tech equipment has boosted share price gains across the technology sector.
But the centres also need power sources, intensive cooling systems, and old-fashioned construction, plumbing and electrical work, all providing money and jobs for local communities and beyond.
Opposition has been building over worries about the environmental and human costs of the huge server farms, including air pollution, higher energy costs, water use and noise.
The Democratic wave in this week’s midterm elections in the United States raised investor fears of a regulatory crackdown — prompting the heavy selling on Wall Street on Thursday.

Markets are pricing in the risk that “Democratic victories in the states with the most projects will make construction more expensive and longer to complete”, said Kevin Thozet at the asset management firm Carmignac in Paris.
American households
Share ownership is widespread in the United States, where individual retirement funds invested in stocks and bonds are much more prevalent than government-funded pensions.
“Forty-three per cent of household wealth is now exposed to the stock market, an increase of 10 percentage points from 2000,” said Cavalier.
A sustained market downturn would directly impact their spending power, especially for retirees, creating a wider economic risk.
And “the richest 10 per cent of Americans now account for half of consumer spending”, said Alexandre Baradez, an analyst at the brokerage IG France.
“They’re the ones who own the most stocks and have benefited the most from the tech stock gains,” he said.

A market crisis could crimp their spending as well, meaning it would no longer compensate for the spending pullback among average Americans since the inflation spike provoked by the US war against Iran.
Capital access?
Rising interest rates complicate the picture, since they lift borrowing costs for the billions of dollars in debt AI firms have taken on to finance the data centre rollout.
“This is not an easy time, with shares falling and high rates on debt markets — and little chance of any easing moves soon by central banks,” Baradez said.
Tighter financial conditions and higher cash needs could make investors wary of putting up more money, or lead them to reduce exposure to the sector.
For Jacques-Aurelien Marcireau at Stilgar, an asset management firm in Paris, American politicians are aware of the risks.
“The truth is that Democrats will be pragmatic: there won’t be any general halt to data centre construction,” he told AFP.
But a slowdown “could even be healthy, by halting the most vulnerable projects”, he said.
IPO anxiety
The tech-heavy Nasdaq index had already wobbled before this week and now is officially in a correction, having fallen around 12 per cent over the past month.
That wiped off US$2.5 trillion in market valuation for Nasdaq companies alone.
Investors now question the prospects for the imminent initial public share offering from Claude-maker Anthropic, which had been tipped to surpass SpaceX’s earlier this year as the biggest ever.
It has reportedly been looking to raise a whopping US$100 billion this month to buy the chips and other equipment for its computing needs, which could have valued the start-up at up to US$2 trillion.
Now it may have to settle for less, potentially complicating its race to dominate the market.
Its rival OpenAI has already pushed back its IPO plans to sometime next year.
“Anthropic will be the big test,” Baradez said. — AFP

ac30c3ff268d6e3d: Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now.

Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. Welcome back to Decoder.
Hey, thanks for having me, man.

I’m excited to talk to you. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. I feel like you and I talked a lot about how all that was working, about election security, all those sorts of things. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You’ve been thinking about this stuff a lot. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Just give me the lay of land right now.

October is traditionally security awareness month. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached.

You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry.
A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November.
I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? Is it Russia? Is it North Korea? Do we know?

It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up. In cyber, the kill chain is the things you do to have an effect on a target. So to steal information, to turn something off, to steal money, to steal Bitcoin.

Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. And then you have a human being go and take that stuff you built and deploy it against either one target — because maybe you’re a government and you’re going against Lockheed Martin or you’re going against another government or you’re a ransomware actor — and you take all that work you did and you deploy it against hundreds or thousands of targets really fast. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. One of the things that’s happening is that these systems are going and they’re so good at finding bugs that they are finding the bugs in real time and writing the exploits in real time.

The system that everybody’s talking about is not the only one, but the system we’re talking about is a thing called ARTEX, which is a Chinese open-source tool that anybody can go look at. There’s an English translation on GitHub that you can check out. And if you power it on the back end by something like an obliterated GLM-5.3, it will let you break into a shocking number of organizations. This started with three South Korean banks. This week, about 200 more companies have been hit. I’ve been helping a couple of companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It is shocking the companies that are getting hit by something you could just download. It has been a long time since you’ve been able to go and just download an open-source tool and break into multi-billion dollar companies. It’s like the ‘90s. That’s-
That’s what I was thinking about. I think about Windows in the late ’90s, early 2000s when it was a security disaster.

I started saying this actually in the beginning of this year, that it’s an incredibly exciting and terrifying time, because the last time it felt like this was when I was a much younger man and I would go to the very early DEFCONs. DEFCON these days is like 40,000–60,000 people. Back then [in the 1990s] it was a couple hundred people and it was one track and you’d go in and somebody would give a talk and you’d leave the room and you’d think, “Every company in the world is vulnerable to this attack.” The difference was that the entire world didn’t run on the internet. You could go do bad things, but you couldn’t ruin the world and you certainly couldn’t automate it in the way you can now.

It’s back to those days where tools you could just get and build yourself could do crazy things. It’s back to the Wild West days. Back in those days, there were a couple hundred people who had those skills and we were all in one room in Las Vegas and most of them were actually good guys. They didn’t want to be criminals. And now you have a much larger ecosystem of people, many of whom live in places where the law enforcement can’t touch and who have a big economic incentive and have access to these tools. The other big thing is they no longer have to use frontier models that have protections, that have logs that are available to law enforcement. My M5 Mac Ultra Studio finally showed up and I’ve been running a quantized obliterated GLM-5.3 and oh my God, what you can do is incredible.

You mentioned the economics of frontier models. The economy of cyber is one of those things that has gotten sophisticated over the years. One of the things that our systems got safer is you could pay the number of people at DEF CON a whole bunch of money to protect all the systems and it was economically smart to pay them to be defenders instead of attackers. I’m just rewinding my own brain through this history. There was a long conversation in our industry about security through obscurity by hiding all the bugs and hiding all the code versus open source and being really transparent. There was an etiquette that developed about how to reveal the bugs and when to give people notification. There were transparency reports and bug bounties.

You could call it an etiquette, you could call it an economy. We built a culture around cybersecurity and cyber defense and how the attackers and defenders would operate. What you are describing changes it all for a whole number of reasons, but the one that sticks out to me is the economics of it. I can go buy a Mac Studio, I can get an open-weight model and I can just start and that does not place me inside of the culture. There’s not going to be some old man, an Obi-Wan Kenobi saying, “Here’s how you act like a cybersecurity Jedi.” I’m just going to start doing stuff. Tell me how that’s changing right now.

And that is when we started designing how we do software security and these big companies, Microsoft and Oracle and then later Amazon and Salesforce and these folks, started hiring ex-hackers. I was part of that generation of the ex-hackers who were at DEF CON and Black Hat and got hired by the companies to go break their stuff. We started coming up with responsible disclosure, bug bounties, consulting companies, so the Foundstone and @stake and then Mandiant and CrowdStrike, these companies grow up and we get this huge industry that is now RSA and Black Hat. This multi-billion dollar security industry grew up in the 2000s and 2010s.

That era is over, like you said, because it was based upon a couple of assumptions. One was that there was a hierarchy of skillsets of people who could do this stuff. You had the script kiddies who could download tools to do things and then the next level up of the people who could write those tools and that was a more rarefied skill set. There were the vulnerability researchers and then there were the gods, and that god tier was in the hundreds of people and those are the people who could do the really, really good vulnerability research, who could write the really, really good shell code, who could reverse engineer patches from Microsoft or somebody like that.

If you wanted to build an attack team, then you have a small R&D component and then you have a much larger operational component. If you were a professional attack team at U.S. Cyber Command, at Russia SVR, at Chinese MSS, that you build the structure of your R&D team of elite people and then your less elite operational people, and that was copied then by the Russian ransomware actors. You have to have a conspiracy of people to do this stuff. A lot of this stuff also fell apart with the invention of Bitcoin because one of the assumptions was that you had to have people who could launder money and Bitcoin meant that nerds could launder money. So that started to change the economics of the entire thing.

All this stuff is falling apart because of AI, because the skillset issue is that now script kiddies have a bunch of the skillset of the Dave Vitales and the other cyber gods who could do these things, such that with this Mac that’s sitting on my desktop, I can reverse engineer a Microsoft patch and walk through and then write stable exploit code. It’s not quite there yet to be automatic. You still have to have a bunch of skills, but we’re really, really close.

What’s really concerning, and what you see with the ARTEX stuff, is you can now kind of let loose on the operational side. We were never secure. It was all a fantasy. These vulnerabilities have always existed. These companies have never been safe. And that is what we’ve seen over the last decade is these mostly Russian ransomware actors nailing the mid-size companies that most people have never heard of that are actually really important, like some midsize industrial company that makes some widget that we all depend upon. It’s because a company like that’s got one security guy and a 10 person, 12 person IT team and they’re going up against a 20 person Russian ransomware team, they’re toast.

But it’s just because there’s only a handful of Russian teams that could do that. Now two or three Russian kids can have a whole bank of Macs or, if they have the money, they can buy Nvidia H-100s and they can run a ton of agents who do this all day and that is what is changing.

I’m sorry, you asked who was doing this. For Binance, it’s North Koreans and they have an entire team where all they do is steal Bitcoin. Other people have gotten out of it because it’s really hard to compete against a foreign intelligence agency that recruits their smartest kids and all they do is steal Bitcoin. We ran a headline ages ago called “Attack of the Killer Script Kiddies” at the very beginning of all this, and I feel bad because it is much more suited to now than it was to then, because then it was just a lot of automated mischief. Now —
Because you wasted the headline. You wish you held it back.

We wasted the headline. Every now and again you get a lightning bolt of a headline. You got to get it out there. It’s a great piece of art. We’ll put it in the show notes, but it feels like the diffusion you’re talking about is not that a bunch of teenagers are going to be even more malicious. It’s a bunch of bad actors with real incentives to do harm are now vastly more capable than they were before. And that doesn’t seem like you can re-jigger the economics of that unless you somehow make it really expensive to do the attacks.
I think it’s going to be extremely hard to make it expensive to do the attacks.

We’re going to have to lower the cost of defense. You’re completely right to look at this economic problem because what’s happening is attacks are becoming agentic. The cost per token for attackers is going towards zero, and the cost of defense for defenders is staying quite high. It is very important for us to find ways for defenders to have cheaper options. I think that is critical. That’s something I am personally extremely focused on. To be frank, very few people are.

There are a couple of problems here. One, there’s a ton of focus on the defensive side of AI on finding and fixing bugs. That’s great. It’s important. But software security as a CISO… I work for an AI software company, Cognition. Even as a CISO of a software product company, software security is 25% of my job. I have all kinds of other responsibilities. And software security is the part of my job that has been both the most revolutionized and the most improved by AI. The other 75% has been helped a bit and in some cases made much worse. There’s so much more we need to do than just hill climb on finding and fixing bugs. There’s been so much less hill climbing on all these other things. And the next area needs to be the operational security side.
Wait, give me an example of the other things, the 75%.

Okay. So the operational security side is watching your logs, saying, “Ah, somebody is running our techs against us. I am now going to trigger an investigation. I am going to look to see what is going on and I’m going to make an intelligent decision of what I am going to do to respond to this without shutting down the entire company.” That is SOC (security operations center) work. Companies that want to survive this era are going to have to replace human beings who do that work with the first tier and then eventually the second tier with AI. And you can do that with current LLMs.

The first tier actually has to be not an LLM. It has to be something much dumber because you’re looking at terabytes or petabytes of logs and it is just completely uneconomical to do that with an actual LLM. We have other things — TF-IDFs, MLBERTs, traditional classifiers — that can operate much faster, but then that sets off an alarm and then you send it to a small LLM and then the small LLM calls its bigger brother and that might call an even bigger brother.

But for those models, we need to do a lot more work to optimize them and we need to make them cheap. I have a colleague who works at one of the large security platform companies who said that doing an investigation on one of the big frontier model cyber models costs $900 on their product to do an investigation. That is not going to work when the Russian ransomware guys are either using Macs or they’re using throwaway crypto mining rigs and their marginal cost is zero.

This is one of the things we’re working on at Cognition: We train our own models, retrain open weights, and we’re trying to drive this cost way down. It’s something we’ve done, but we have a lot more work to do here and a lot of other people have work to do here. This is where, as an industry, we have to focus on the Pareto frontier between cost and efficiency on cyber because it’s not just bug-finding.

The other place here is, people talk about Mythos. Mythos is great, Astra Cyber is great. They’re incredible models, but even the people who have access to it, which is a tiny number of companies, they only scan their most important code. And there are hundreds of billions of lines of code out there that are not the Linux kernel, that are the crap C# and J2E code that was written by Infosys 15 years ago. All of that code is not going to go through a frontier cyber model that costs a gazillion dollars. That’s the kind of stuff that we need to work on cost efficiency for.

It feels like you’re describing this cliche that I hear all the time: Everything’s going to get so much worse before it gets totally secure forever. And it doesn’t seem like the model you’re describing leads to that result. We’re not going to fix all the bugs forever in some valley of despair and then always have perfect code. At some point, there’s some cost advantage to the attacker, always. You’re running a company, you can’t write defense that has zero marginal costs. Someone has to do it even if the attackers are so infinite that their marginal cost is effectively zero. So are we going to go through a period where everything is so much worse and then it’s perfect forever? Or how does the cost manage itself out, into balance?
0f0e00fd4a24ced0: Fireworks AI is fine with helping companies run AI models in their own datacenters, though VP Rob Ferguson argues against doing so.

Ferguson told The Register in an interview that while Fireworks AI, a managed inference provider, supports on-prem AI, "we're trying to push people more and more away from it because frankly, it's just the economics."
The GPU hardware is just so expensive that if you can't keep it fully utilized, it's a waste of money, he contends. Ten thousand GPUs, he said, represent a billion dollars of capital.
"You don't want those things to be sitting idle," he said.

For companies with particularly sensitive workloads, Ferguson said, Fireworks is happy to work something out – it offers a service called Sovereign for just that purpose and it has partners like Microsoft that can help. But most inference work probably doesn't need that level of protection, he said.

"The state of the art for everyone is to have a portfolio of models," he explained. "In fact, I think most people don't know that the best model in the world's not Astra. The best model in the world's not Fable. The best model is literally a portfolio and we can prove it. You are always better routing between a few models than to do one singular model."

That's what Fireworks does through Nexus and its API, alongside competitors like Together AI, Baseten, and DeepInfra. As a managed inference platform, Fireworks AI routes inference tasks to whichever model, frontier model subscription, or API is best suited to handle them.
But the company is not just doing naive routing like an AI gateway. It's evaluating tasks as they come in and directing them to the optimal model.

"We build custom routers," Ferguson explained. "Our auto model is continuously updating so that we actually go through and we grade the difficulty of the task and we see if there're affinities that the models have, like Kimi is slightly better at JavaScript than Python, things like this."
The company's competitive edge, he contends, is its crack engineering team, which follows from its founders' work on PyTorch, a widely used open source machine learning library.

"We're performance experts both on the training and inference side," he explained. "People I think don't understand how important, for example, numerics is. So when you use a model, it's always called a mixture of experts – an expert is a different machine.

"And so you have all these different machines. It actually matters when you're training that you go back to precisely the right machine, because if you don't, the other machine will still answer the question, but it'll answer in a slightly different way. So we have to know how to build the topology to write back the data to the right space. We have to understand floating point precision [to handle very small values]. We have to be able to do all this where we're routing through a complex fabric through potentially more than one provider depending on what everything is. And so we're really systems experts."

Hyperscalers, he argues, will give you a GPU but then it's your responsibility to put it to use. Fireworks' advantage involves being able to maximize utilization at scale while maintaining model precision and speed.
Ferguson said AI keeps coming back to economics.

"People are just trying to figure out more and more things to use AI for and [to answer questions like] just how much more can I send to cached models, how much more can I send to open models, when do I need this specialization?" he said. "So we're constantly working with customers to help them come up with their own evaluation criteria."

One reason for this, Ferguson explained, is that frontier model companies are not transparent about their caching rates. He said Fireworks was working with a data science company and was caching about 90 percent of the tasks.

"We looked at [Anthropic's] Opus and it was caching 30 percent of the time," he said. "It was doing AI rework constantly. And with AI, rework is by far your biggest cost. If it's not hitting a cache, then your costs are absolutely insane. And so the token cost is not the real cost. It's the cost per task. And they're hiding that from you. And so we always tell our customers to be tracking cost per task, because that's the real number."
Another factor that companies should consider in their cost calculations, Ferguson suggested, is the value of their data and whether they're giving that data away for training.
"I think people grossly underestimate the value of their data," he said.

Fireworks AI has a zero data-retention policy, "but a lot of times," Ferguson said, "these other companies [do] not, and you should be getting paid for your data. Nobody really knew at the beginning of this current era that these models are memorizers. But now there's plenty of evidence that these models are. So if they're going to be using your data, then you should be getting value for it."
But it's not just about cost. Speed, said Ferguson, is underappreciated.

"Speed is the thing that people often don't know they can ask for," he said. "It's such a game changer for me and how I work with AI is so different when the responses come back as fast as I ask them."
What's the advantage of model ensembling, as the company refers to its model routing activities? A bill that's at least 50 percent smaller, Ferguson claims.

"So we say six to eight times cheaper," he said. "The reality is that because a lot of folks have a preference in their tooling, we kinda guarantee that in the case where you're still using a combo of closed and open models, we can always guarantee that your bill will drop by half right away. Like we're sure about that. And then the question is can we just get you to use more stuff?" ®

16a91ca9fca2c937: WASHINGTON, Nov 7 — Production of Cybertrucks — the pickups hailed by enthusiasts as a symbol of Elon Musk’s futuristic ambitions and equally hated as ugly reminders of the Donald Trump era — will wind down, the Tesla CEO said yesterday.
Tesla will stop building the truck at its Texas factory around the middle of 2027 to free up space for its Cybercab robotaxi, Musk said.
“Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production,” Musk wrote on X.
Musk did not say whether the truck would be built elsewhere or discontinued altogether, nor what would happen to outstanding orders.
Wes Morrill, the Cybertruck’s lead engineer, wrote in a separate post that the truck “was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab.”
“Thanks to everyone who contributed to making the future (look) like the future,” he added.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Tesla Cybertruck electric vehicles sit parked in a storage lot in San Diego, California on April 11, 2025. — AFP pic
Tesla fans lamented the departure of the Cybertruck on X, the social media platform Musk owns, but the tycoon reassured them that the Cybertruck fleet “will be around for a long time.”

The truck came to be seen as an extension of Musk himself, and its image became entangled with his politics as he took on a high-profile role leading the Trump administration’s cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency. Some owners reported vandalism and harassment.
The angular stainless-steel behemoth was unveiled in November 2019, and Musk said at the time it had drawn 250,000 preorders within days.
Production was originally slated for 2021 but was repeatedly delayed, with customer deliveries starting in late 2023.
Tesla built its Texas lines with planned capacity of 250,000 trucks a year, but sales have come nowhere near that figure.
As US demand slumped, Tesla began selling the truck abroad, starting deliveries in South Korea in November 2025 and in the United Arab Emirates in January.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Tesla electric cars and a Cybertruck are displayed in a test drive vehicle charging area at a shopping mall parking garage in San Diego, California, on April 23, 2025. — AFP pic
Tesla does not break out Cybertruck revenue, but its “other models” category, which includes the pickup, accounts for just a small percentage of sales.
Cox Automotive estimated total sales of just 72,702, with more than half in 2024 and fading thereafter.
The truck has also been subject to multiple recalls and complaints over build quality.
The Cybercab, a two-seat vehicle with no steering wheel or pedals, was unveiled in October 2024.
Tesla began production at the Texas plant in April and started offering paid Cybercab rides in Austin in September through its existing Robotaxi service.

“The decision to discontinue the Cybertruck highlights how difficult it can be to translate strong initial attention and enthusiasm around a new vehicle into sustainable mainstream demand,” said Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive.
Tesla saw the vehicle as a bid for the giant US pickup truck market, but it quickly became a “niche” product, Valdez Streaty said.

The robotaxi is central to Musk’s effort to recast Tesla as an artificial intelligence and robotics company rather than a carmaker, though its success depends on the company delivering fully driverless technology, which it has yet to demonstrate at scale. — AFP

<!--kg-card-end: html--> Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that drew a blank, felt the squeeze, played the queen, and made donkey-bull love.

First, scientists shed new light on how Earth ended up losing more than a billion years of its geological record, a puzzle that has resisted explanation for decades. Then: octopuses in tight spots, a topless spear-brandishing Celt, and a tale of unlikely tail.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files.
“Blank Space” (Earth’s Version)
Dhungana, Santosh and Flament, Nicolas. “The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity. Nature.

Earth doesn’t trouble itself too much with keeping intact archives. With its tectonic activity and erosive forces, our planet is constantly wiping out huge chunks of its own memory, creating gaps in the geological record called unconformities.

The Great Unconformity, the largest gap of this kind, reveals that Earth straight-up deleted more than a billion years of strata, for reasons that remain hotly debated and mysterious. Sandstone that dates back to the Cambrian period some 538 million years is often found directly on top of ancient “basement” rocks that date back anywhere from 1.2 billion to 1.8 billion years ago. This missing layer shows up around the world, hinting that it was erased by a global event.
Now, scientists have placed the origins of the Great Unconformity deep inside Earth’s mantle, during the tectonic tumult of supercontinent breakup.

“The cause or causes of the Great Unconformity are unknown,” said authors Santosh Dhungana and Nicolas Flament of the University of Wollongong. “The proposed mechanisms include extensive glacial erosion during Snowball Earth (about 720–635 million years ago), rifting and plume activity, sea-level fall and mantle-driven dynamic topography.”
“These processes have not been dynamically tested, with limited comparison between global models and global datasets to explain the spatial distribution of the Great Unconformity,” the team added.

To fill the knowledge gap about the geological gap, the researchers ran models of the formation and breakup of ancient supercontinents during the eons preceding the Cambrian period, when complex life rapidly proliferated in Earth’s seas. Massive landmasses were pushed upward by motions in Earth’s mantle during this time. Exposed to erosive forces such as weather, glaciers, and eventually oceans, they became sanded down over time, creating the vast void.

“Our models explain why the Great Unconformity is best preserved in North America and show that it is a first-order surface expression of deep geodynamic processes that transformed global landscapes and sediment fluxes,” the team concluded.

Scientists will no doubt continue to debate the cause of this planet-wide memory lapse, but there is consensus that the same mechanisms also set the stage for the emergence of complex life during the Cambrian. No matter what caused the Great Unconformity, we partly owe our existence to it today.
In other news…
Putting the squeeze on octopuses
Xin, Wenci et al. “Overcoming environmental constraints: octopus uses 3-step or 4-step strategies to squeeze through small holes.” Journal of Experimental Biology.

We’ll move now from massive gaps in Earth’s memory to tiny gaps that octopuses can somehow squeeze through. These tentacled escape artists can famously maneuver their way through passages that seem impossibly small relative to their bodies, an ability that has spawned a subgenre of viral videos.

Now, scientists have discovered the secrets of “octopus-squeezing behavior” by observing two species—the common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) and the Mayan octopus (Octopus maya)—navigating small holes in laboratory containers.

“Our study demonstrates that octopuses employ two primary strategies, 3-step and 4-step, for squeezing through narrow spaces,” said researchers led by Wenci Xin of the National University of Singapore. “The key distinction between these strategies lies in whether the body is squeezed separately from the arms.”

The first two steps were probing the aperture and then shifting a few arms through it. Navigating the tightest spaces required breaking up the final passage into two parts: Pulling the remaining arms to the other side, and then compressing the mantle behind the head so they could fit through last.
In addition to documenting these amazing feats of flexibility in nature, the study is the perfect excuse to revisit the classic X-Files episode “Squeeze.”
A queen hidden in plain sight?
Russell, Miles. “Verica Rex: Searching for a ‘lost’ queen of the British Iron Age.” Current Archaeology.

When Rome invaded Britain 2,000 years ago, they had the help of an inside man—or was it an inside woman? In a new article, an archaeologist makes the case that the British king Verica, who aided the Roman invasion of their own homeland, was actually a queen that has been misgendered lo these many centuries.

Miles Russell of Bournemouth University argues that Verica was a woman based in part on the leader’s Latin name, which ends in the suffix “a” which is common for women, as opposed to names ending in “-us” for men.

Coins also depict Verica using “slender, bare-breasted equestrian figures that appear irrefutably female in contrast to the overtly masculine warriors on the issues of Iron Age rulers like Tasciovanus and Caratacus,” according to Russell.

Many experts are not convinced that the evidence points to a secret ancient queen, and Verica’s gender is likely to inspire much more debate. Wikipedia, our great public arbiter, has not changed Verica’s male pronouns.

Women leaders weren’t unheard of in Celtic Britain, as evidenced by the queens Cartimandua and Boudica, who lived in the same century as Verica. Regardless of whether Verica was among their ranks, this leader was a consequential figure in the Roman takeover of Britain.
Achille and Patroclo: More than friends
Da Cruz, André B et al. “A socio-sexual bond between a bull and a male donkey.” Current Biology.
Scientists who were conducting fieldwork on monkeys in Ethiopia serendipitously stumbled upon a very different discovery—a tender same-sex relationship between a bull and a donkey.

Achille, a bull, and Patroclo, a donkey, belong to different owners, but they graze together by day. Despite the availability of other males and females in their pasture, this pair has developed a strong socio-sexual bond that includes nuzzling, licking, and Achille sexually mounting Patroclo.

“Patroclo frequently presented his hindquarters toward Achille and nipped him,” said researchers led by André Beirão da Cruz of the University of Pisa. “In the only two instances in which Achille approached and mounted another male donkey, this individual showed clear avoidance behaviours and displayed threatening facial expressions (e.g. ear flattening), which were never observed in Patroclo during the 51 mountings (34 with intromission) with Achille.”

Same-sex sexual behavior is extremely common in nature and has a wide variety of possible explanations, including social cohesion, mistaken identity, or lack of access to opposite-sex mates. But what Achille and Patroclo have is special. Despite being different species and having alternate mating options, the pair share a highly selective and reciprocal social and sexual bond.

“Although interpreting this behaviour is challenging, the mounting attempts, taken together with the repeated and mutual affiliative interactions between the two animals, may signal the quality of their relationship” and “the strength of the animals’ social bond,” the team concluded.

In addition to this heartwarming tale, the study goes to show that you never know what you might find when you chase your goals. The researchers were there to watch geladas, but it turned out those primates weren’t the only animals monkeying around.
Thanks for reading! See you next week.

f6a76a717d926501: It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters.

At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors.

Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads.

6e008ea4482d46e8: NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review has found.

The report [PDF] comes almost exactly a year after the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust disclosed a data breach affecting 8,003 people, including current and former trust staff and non-trust workers.

A member of the public discovered the exposure in November 2025. An Excel workbook published in response to a Freedom of Information request in February 2023 retained underlying sickness absence records that users could reveal through its pivot tables.
Staff assigned to the helpline described difficult calls involving shouting, anger, and distress.

Particularly difficult calls involved people distressed by the sensitivity of the disclosures or potentially in danger from domestic abuse. Call handlers said they had to make safeguarding assessments without training or an established process.
"Such occurrences of anger or distress were not infrequent, and this reflected the heightened emotions and distress experienced by callers to varying degrees due to the breach," the review noted.
"This placed significant emotional burden on individuals working in the contact center, who were not prepared or provided support on how to deal with those."

Members of the trust's clinical governance team were told just a day beforehand that they would staff the helpline. Despite their experience dealing with patient trauma, they received little preparation for the calls that followed.

"The staff working in the call centers had a short training session and then the calls started coming in within minutes of the team being set up," the review noted. "Some staff had not finished reading the pre-prepared script which had arrived only 30 minutes before the center went live."
Most call handlers only learned that their own data had been exposed while already working on the helpline, sometimes minutes before supporting others affected.
Call handlers also said they had little choice about taking on the work and were expected to maintain their usual duties alongside it.
The review stated that some staff members gave up weekends and worked long past their scheduled hours to meet the demands of both roles.
"It's typical NHS, it runs on goodwill," one staffer told the team that compiled the report.
The call center was only supposed to run for two weeks in December 2025, but due to the volume of calls, it was eventually stood down after 11 weeks, in February 2026.
According to officials speaking at a trust board meeting on Thursday, the review and its findings have since been circulated among staff, and published online.
How the spreadsheet slipped through

Responding to a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request thought to be from a journalist researching a story about stress in the NHS, the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust uploaded a spreadsheet to its public FOI Disclosure log in February 2023.

This contained personal data and inadvertently exposed sickness absence information and sensitive health data related to 7,715 staff, 288 non-trust workers, as well as a small number of unidentified records.

Crucially, this spreadsheet was uploaded in a format that allowed users to access the pivot table from which some data was derived. The data in these pivot tables would normally have been too sensitive to be included in FOIA responses.

The first failure was that the request was handled by the trust's e-Rostering team instead of the People Information Unit, which had the expertise in responding to FOIA requests with complex datasets.
The e-Rostering team compiled the response using the team's own data, but incorrectly believed they had stripped the spreadsheet of the sensitive data that would later be exposed.
Standard procedures instructed request handlers to follow several steps to ensure sensitive data was stripped before documents are published, some of which were skipped.

For starters, one FOI officer assigned to the response either failed to run the spreadsheet through Excel's Document Inspector, which formed part of the usual procedures, or failed to act upon its recommendations.
This feature can flag pivot tables and potentially hidden cached data, but cannot determine whether that data is sensitive or automatically remove the cache.

Staff also failed to follow instructions to convert the spreadsheet to PDF. Investigators found that doing so prevented users clicking through to the underlying records, although they could not guarantee that no hidden data remained technically accessible.
At the time, internal guidance did not require conversion to CSV, which would have removed the workbook's pivot-table functionality and embedded cache.

The trust's sign-off process also focused on answering the request's questions and meeting their public relations duties, and falsely assumed that the data had been adequately sanitized before the final review.
The spreadsheet was made available for 33 months, although the trust is not sure how many times it was viewed during that time.

Its logs only covered the 12 months before a member of the public alerted it to the pivot table issue. These indicated that it had been accessed 340 times, although the review noted there was no way of knowing how many of these, if any, led to pivot tables being accessed, or even if it was viewed by a human, with web crawlers adding to the total view count.
The trust has since implemented a number of changes to prevent a recurrence of the breach, including the mandatory password-protecting of any Excel workbook as part of FOIA responses.

A senior information governance officer must now approve spreadsheet responses before executive sign-off. Revised guidance circulated in November 2025 also called for conversion to CSV, although investigators found that this requirement had not been incorporated into the formal operating procedure and recommended updating it.
The review says the Information Commissioner's Office closed its case after the trust implemented its recommendations.

A spokesperson for the Royal Cornwall Hospitals said: "We are deeply sorry for the accidental sharing of sickness absence data which we reported in November 2025, and for the distress and concern it caused those colleagues whose data was involved.

57b9d6362f0d80bf: And helping to make the goals for EU accession plausible
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot from the EkoMapa website of the EkoGard organization in Montenegro. Fair use.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Montenegro is on its way to joining the EU; at the moment, the goal is to do so by 2028. The United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) review in 2025 states that the country has made significant progress in aligning its environmental legal and regulatory framework, as well as much of its national legislation, with European Union (EU) directives.
However, some problems remain, including waste management and a very low recycling rate — less than 2 percent, far below the EU’s 50 percent target.

Austrian Member of Parliament Thomas Waitz (Greens/EFA), chair of the delegation to the EU-Montenegro Stabilisation and Association Parliamentary Committee, said in an interview with The New Union Post that there have been “massive improvements” in Montenegro, citing as an example the closure of more than 100 illegal landfills in the last year: “It is a great effort for such a small country. But they have another 500, and if we expected them to have them all cleaned up, it would be impossible.”

While politicians and international agencies discuss how Montenegro could get closer to the target and put its waste management under control, ordinary citizens are making practical steps to improve the situation today.
This Digital Spark spotlight story is about one such organization, EkoGard, and the many people who participate in its efforts and, step by step, try to make Montenegro cleaner.
Global Voices interviewed the organization’s founder and general director, Senad Pepić, about the impact of Digital Spark and its community initiative.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project.

Senad Pepić (SP): EkoGard was built through years of work on the ground, not in an office. It grew out of the Očistimo Rožaje initiative, where we spent six years building a strong community of people ready to take action. We started with illegal dumpsites, but our work gradually expanded to other environmental and social issues affecting everyday life.
We organized cleanups, worked with young people, launched campaigns, and encouraged residents to tackle problems that kept coming back.

We joined Digital Spark because we wanted to bring what we learned in the field together with digital tools and data. We hoped to show a fuller picture of the problems and change how people talk about them. EkoMapa grew out of that idea as a natural next step in our work.
GV: What issue or challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

SP: One cleanup in particular made us rethink our approach. We cleared an illegal dumpsite beside a rural road, in an area where residents had no suitable place to dispose of their waste. The nearest legal disposal point was about six kilometers away.

After the cleanup, we asked for a waste container to be installed and were promised that the problem would be addressed. Three years passed; the container was never installed, and the dumpsite returned.

Its return changed how we saw similar sites elsewhere. We had photos, posts, and letters from other areas, but no way to see the full extent of the problem or how it related to gaps in waste collection services.

We wanted to map these places and understand the conditions in each settlement. Doing that gives us a way to show local institutions where waste disposal services are lacking and talk about what needs to change.
GV: What are the key changes or activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

SP: Before this project, EkoGard organized cleanups, worked with young people, held educational activities, ran campaigns, and drew attention to local problems. Through Digital Spark, we began collecting and analysing what we saw in the field more systematically.

EkoMapa started as a map of illegal dumpsites, but it grew into a tool for understanding environmental conditions across the community. We decided to look at conditions settlement by settlement, so we could connect the problems we found with the services available to residents.

We also developed a model that uses the information we collect to assess environmental risks and gaps in local services in each settlement. It helps us spot patterns, compare needs across settlements, and discuss what the data shows with local institutions.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.
SP: Our activists now have a practical tool and a clearer way to document what they find. We can use that information in public campaigns and make a stronger case for change.
For residents, we can now show how the problems they face relate to the services available in their settlements.
Organizations from other towns and countries have also shown interest in using the tool to understand conditions in their own communities and involve residents in finding solutions.

The local waste management company has also recognized that the information could be useful in its work. For now, the clearest changes are in how our activists work and in the conversations we have begun with other organizations and local institutions. Changes on the ground will take longer.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

SP: Through the project, we learned that giving people a way to report a problem is only a first step. They also need to know why we collect the information, what we will do with it, and how it might lead to change.
The training on how to reach people and communicate more clearly was especially useful. It made us think about the words we use and how to talk about problems without making people feel powerless.

For us, digital democracy means residents can help identify problems and take part in finding solutions. When we collect, check, and present what they tell us clearly, it can inform our campaigns and conversations with institutions. It also helps us ask for clearer answers.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

SP: The most valuable lesson is that technology cannot solve a problem on its own. It can help us see what is happening across a community, but it cannot replace fieldwork, talking with residents, or working with institutions.
Finding a problem on a map is just the beginning. We also need to understand why it happened. If we only deal with what we can see, the same problem is likely to return.

When we bring the data together with people’s experiences, we can start to propose solutions that meet their needs. That is what we will take into our future work: listen, look for patterns and causes, and use what we learn to push for change.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

SP: Our next step is to present our findings to the local government and make the case for better planning of waste collection and other local services. We want to draw attention to settlements that have been overlooked for years and follow up on how institutions respond.

We are already applying what we learned to EkoGard’s wider work, especially our campaigns and how we involve residents. Together with other organizations from Montenegro, we are preparing a campaign to establish a National Eco Line, a nationwide channel for reporting environmental problems and following up on how the responsible authorities respond.
We know the results may take time, so we will keep working with other organizations and local institutions.
Written by Daria Dergacheva

ca8187dc18d8d6b4: From P Kamalanathan

Deepavali is here again. In every Hindu home, the oil lamps are lit, the kolam is drawn, the house is filled with the smell of murukku, nei urundai and payasam, and children run around in new clothes, waiting for the first burst of fireworks.
But beyond the celebration, Deepavali carries a timeless message that we must never forget: Light must triumph over darkness.
Thiruvalluvar said it beautifully more than 2,000 years ago:
Those who seek the Divine will be freed from the darkness of life.
That darkness is not just outside us. It is also within us; anger, jealousy, hatred, selfishness, and division.
Deepavali reminds us to light a lamp inside ourselves first.
Deepavali is also a celebration of our identity

For Malaysians of Indian origin, Deepavali is not just a festival. It is a reminder of who we are, where we come from, and what we carry forward for our children. Our language, our culture, our values, our faith, these are the lamps we must keep burning.

Just this week, we saw how important it is to protect that light. When there was a proposal to reduce Tamil language hours in our Tamil schools from 12 to 10 periods, our community spoke up together; teachers, parents, PTAs, leaders, and ordinary families. And I am grateful that the education ministry listened and decided not to pursue it.
That is the spirit of Deepavali. When we stand together in light, darkness cannot win.
Deepavali is a Malaysian celebration

In Malaysia, Deepavali is not celebrated only by Indians. Our Malay, Chinese, Kadazan, Iban and Orang Asli friends join us at our open houses, taste our food, wear Indian clothes, and share our joy. That is the true beauty of Malaysia, unity in diversity, not just in words, but in our homes.

As a former deputy education minister, I have always believed that our greatest strength is our children. If we teach them to respect all races and religions, to love their own mother tongue while embracing Bahasa Malaysia and English, to be kind and to be disciplined; then Malaysia’s future will be bright.
This Deepavali, let us make three promises:
1. Light a lamp for unity Let us reject hatred and division, and choose understanding.
2. Light a lamp for education Let us encourage our children to study hard, to read our mother tongue language, to master knowledge, and to be proud of their heritage.
3. Light a lamp for kindness Let us remember the poor, the lonely, and those who are struggling. Share a meal. Visit an old folks’ home. Help a neighbour. That is the true Deepavali.
To all Malaysians, I wish you a Happy Deepavali.
May your home be filled with light, your family with love, and your life with health and prosperity.
P Kamalanathan is a former deputy education minister and an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
