1c4079f29568663f: Linux Mint 27 is expected next month, and it's starting to take shape. Its flagship desktop, Cinnamon 2.8, is already available.

The team behind the popular, beginner-friendly Linux just released Cinnamon 2.8, which will be the default desktop in Mint 27. Since 2014, Linux Mint versions have been based on the LTS releases of Ubuntu. Since a new LTS, Ubuntu 26.04 "Resolute Raccoon" arrived in late April, that means that a corresponding version of Mint is in development.

The Mint project blog post last month revealed the codename: "Adrien." This is the first male codename since Mint 1.0 "Ada" in 2006, based on the first ever Ubuntu LTS release, 6.06 "Dapper Drake", but the project has run through the whole alphabet since then (except for the letter “Y”.) That blog also revealed it will have a new alarm clock app, but the subsequent Mint Blog post imparted more information.

The Nemo file manager will gain a preview pane, there will be a new and much more capable system resource-monitor program called "Superlight", a new simple manager for compressed archive files (Zip and so on) called "Unfold," and a new, theme-able terminal emulator called "Velocitty." Mint also has a new Community Website, which uses GitHub to manage logins and eliminates the old website's dependency on PHP.

Probably the most significant new feature, though, is that Mint 27 will restore system hibernation. Ubuntu supported hibernation in its early releases, but it has been disabled as standard since 12.04 "Precise Pangolin." Enabling it again is regularly discussed, for instance back in 2020. As we discussed in some detail a year ago, it's a complicated subject and there's a lot that can go wrong.

It seems that Mint's Clément Lefebvre feels he can sort this, and we hope it works out. Support is included in the new version of Cinnamon, among a host of other changes. Its Wayland support is no longer experimental, although the X11 session is still there so users won't be forced to use the new system. The Network Manager applet has better, simpler VPN support and Wi-Fi encryption handling. There are multiple improvements across the desktop: better handling of sound devices, keyboard input layouts, touchpads and gesture support, HiDPI display handling, and better search in the Settings app. The window list control has been upgraded, more things happen in the background for faster desktop starts, and it has better handling and storage of authentication and credentials, including the same Rust-based "oo7" secret store we mentioned in Fedora 45. Screensaver handling is also mentioned – this is particularly problematic under Wayland, as XScreensaver maintainer Jamie Zawinski has covered with some feeling. The Mint blog mentioned this at the start of 2026, when Lefebvre announced the new, slower, annual release schedule.

Cinnamon is not the only desktop environment that has moved to embrace Wayland while also maintaining its support for X.org. Almost exactly two years ago, we reported that the LXQt 2.1 included preliminary Wayland support. That project is very much still in active development, led by Jen-Lee "PCMan" Hong, and version 2.5.0 just appeared, almost simultaneously with Cinnamon 2.8.

Before LXQt, "PCMan" developed the LXDE desktop – which is still around. There's an LXDE spin of Fedora 45, the Raspberry Pi OS uses some of its components, and last year when Debian 13 was released we also noted that its terminal emulator, LXTerminal, had just been updated. This release of LXQt removes its last dependency on an LXDE component – until now, it still used the old menu-cache.

LXQt 2.5 is based on Qt 6.10, and it draws upon some of the components of KDE Plasma. One of these is libkscreen, which manages screens for Plasma. Version 6.8 of this drops X11 support – as does Plasma 6.8 itself – and that broke LXQt's Monitor Settings applet. The team are looking for a workaround and plan to fix this in a minor point release. Aside from this, the desktop's taskbar-style panel has improved sizing support, icon handling, and auto-hide, but most of the improvements in this release are in around its QTerminal terminal emulator.
New LXQt versions usually appear twice a year, around April and November, so this version will likely be in Lubuntu 27.04 in about five months – and available in many other distributions, too. ®

a3ed6642a70163d5: WASHINGTON: Employment in the US grew by 165,000 jobs in October, far exceeding analysts' expectations, with the unemployment rate dipping to 4.1%, government data showed on Friday.

The relatively stable labour market has allowed the US Federal Reserve – which has a dual mandate to maintain inflation at a long-term 2% target while ensuring maximum employment – to make fighting stubbornly high prices its priority.
The strong October data could add to pressure for further rate hikes.

That would put the Fed at odds with President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly called for lower borrowing costs and responded to the central bank's rate hike in September by demanding, "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!"
Analysts had expected 65,000 new jobs and the unemployment rate to hold at 4.2%, according to a consensus forecast from Briefing.com.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) also revised up job figures for August and September by a combined 84,000 jobs, the department said in a statement.
The revision to September's data showed that the world's largest economy added 60,000 jobs that month, as opposed to 29,000 as previously reported.
"This is a strong report and a real sign of momentum in the labour market," said Ger Doyle, North America regional president at staffing firm ManpowerGroup.

"Demand is clearly picking up in parts of the economy, but we need to see it spread into more industries and create more opportunities for workers before we call this a broader hiring recovery," he added.
The data comes days after midterm elections in which the cost of living weighed heavily on voters.
October's gain was well above the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, the BLS said.
Professional and business services led the gains, adding 70,000 jobs, far above the sector's average monthly gain of 15,000 over the past year.
Health care added 42,000 jobs, above its average monthly gain of 31,000 over the last year.
The sector has propped up the labour market in the US in the last year, as an ageing population requires more care both in hospitals and at home.
Transportation and warehousing added 25,000 jobs, mostly among couriers and messengers, while manufacturing added 19,000 jobs, the data showed.
Employment in other major sectors, including construction, retail, financial activities and government, was largely unchanged.

Average hourly earnings for all employees were up 3.1% over the past 12 months, the BLS said, with wages continuing to lag behind stubbornly high inflation, meaning most workers are seeing real wage losses.
Raising interest rates tends to cool inflation but can also limit economic activity, which can affect the job market.

80b0fe9799041a2c: DigiCert has admitted that a botched server migration left an internal system exposed to the internet for more than a year, allowing an unauthorized user to access customer data, including passports, driver's licenses, and other identity documents.
The certificate authority has begun notifying affected customers but has yet to disclose how many people had their information exposed.

In an email seen by The Register, DigiCert confirmed the compromised information included names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses. Some records may also have contained passports, driver's licenses, utility bills, or other identification documents.

"We are completing a review of identification documents to determine the specific individuals involved," DigiCert told those affected, adding that it would notify those people once the review was complete.

DigiCert's incident report traces the blunder back to February 2025, when an internal business system was moved from a VPN-protected network to a different availability zone. That change also opened the system up to the public internet, where it sat for more than 16 months without DigiCert realizing.

The archive used the same account management platform as DigiCert's customer-facing products, including a self-registration feature that was never supposed to be available on the internal system. This allowed outsiders to create accounts without multifactor authentication and, thanks to a separate permissions flaw, use them to browse archived customer records.

DigiCert found the unauthorized accounts on June 18, 2026, but initially dismissed them as harmless because they weren't assigned to an application. A security researcher raised the alarm about the account creation issue three days later, but it took until July 2 for DigiCert to shut it down.
Unfortunately, someone had already been poking around.

It wasn't until October 12 that DigiCert began investigating whether customer information had actually been accessed. On October 19, it confirmed that an unauthorized account had accessed a subset of archived records between June 27 and July 2.

DigiCert described the affected records as a "small proportion" of its archive but hasn't disclosed how many customers or individuals were caught up in the breach. The company did not respond to The Register’s questions at the time of publication.

DigiCert's postmortem makes for uncomfortable reading. The server move didn't get a proper security review, monitoring failed to pick up suspicious activity, and the access controls weren't much use against self-registered accounts. The company has since switched off self-registration, tightened network access, and added monitoring that might have come in handy a few months earlier.

Certificate authority operations, CertCentral, and DigiCert ONE were unaffected, the company said, adding that customer credentials and issued certificates remain secure. It also found no evidence that the unauthorized account had been used to issue, revoke, or validate certificates.
That’s good news for anyone worried about their certificates, but less so for those who handed DigiCert a copy of their passport. ®
3a8fc5690275a1d0: Millions of hunters will be in fields and wooded areas, where they can help spot and report any signs of screwworm. Michigan Department of Natural ResourcesFor the first time in over 50 years, an infestation of the flesh-eating fly known as the New World screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax) is spreading on the U.S. mainland, and it is putting livestock and other animals at risk. The New World screwworm doesn’t just attack cattle. All warm-blooded animals are susceptible, including deer and elk, as well as small game, waterfowl and pets. That means hunters headed to the field this fall may be the most important line of defense for spotting this destructive parasite and keeping it from spreading further. As co-directors of the Mississippi State University deer lab, we believe the country’s millions of hunters can serve as a powerful early warning system by keeping a close eye on the state of wildlife they see. Wildlife agencies are already asking them to be vigilant and report any signs of screwworm infestations. The problem with screwworm Unlike other blowflies, New World screwworm larvae feed on living tissue rather than dead tissue. They lay eggs in open wounds or mucosal openings, such as the eyes and nose of livestock, deer or elk. Screwworm larvae are fairly small but destructive. USDA Screwworm larvae later become flies. USDA Wounds as small as tick bites or scratches, as well as natural openings such as the umbilical stump on newborns or on deer’s pedicles, where their antlers grow and are shed, can attract these parasites. Once the eggs hatch, the maggots burrow into the animal’s flesh and feed, enlarging the wound and attracting more flies. Over time, this leads to infection and death. How the US eradicated screwworm in the past All warm-blooded animals are susceptible to the New World screwworm, but America has seen firsthand the harm they can cause to livestock. In the 1950s, livestock producers in the U.S. Southwest lost up to US$100 million annually to New World screwworm infections, equivalent to over $1 billion today. The New World screwworm fly lays its eggs in fresh wounds, where its larvae hatch and eat the flesh. Judy Gallagher/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY The nation was eventually able to eradicate the New World screwworm from the mainland in 1966 using a combination of treating infected animals and raising hundreds of millions of sterilized male flies and releasing them in infested areas. The New World screwworm has a life cycle of only about 21 days, and each female mates only once. Because of that, inundating areas with sterile male flies for a few months, which equates to a few generations of flies, can eradicate a screwworm population. Historical economic impact estimates of New World screwworm cases in the United States before 2025. USDA 2025 Over time, sterile flies were used to push the New World screwworm further south, where they had been contained behind the Darién Gap, Panama’s narrow border region with Colombia. Sterile flies kept the parasite south of Panama for years, but the movement of cattle and wildlife likely brought it north again. Since 2022, the parasites have been reproducing and moving farther northward. There have been hundreds of detections in Mexico and now in the U.S. The Florida Key deer infestation Wildlife have received far less attention than livestock during screwworm infestations, with one exception: In July 2016, the New World screwworm was detected in the Florida Keys in an endangered deer population: the Florida Key deer (Odocoileus virginianus clavium). Signs of a New World screwworm infestation in an animal’s wound. USDA At the time, the Florida Key deer population was estimated at only about 800 to 1,000 individuals. Because they were endangered and isolated, primarily on the islands of Big Pine Key and No Name Key, they were monitored more closely than most wildlife. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service biologists established quarantine zones. They inspected more than 16,900 animals – dogs, cats, a pig and a raccoon were also found with larvae – and they released 150 million sterile flies across the area. The islands lost 9% to 20% of the total Key Deer population, but the New World screwworm was declared eradicated there on March 23, 2017, less than a year after it was discovered. Screwworm is back In June 2026, screwworm was back in the United States. A rancher discovered the first New World screwworm case in a calf near La Pryor, Texas. A few more cases were confirmed in livestock and domestic animals in Texas and New Mexico. The number of cases in animals had passed 120 as of Nov. 7, 2026, including in two elk reported by hunters in Texas. The U.S. government has started ramping up production of sterile flies to try to keep the parasites from spreading. The state of Texas encouraged ranchers and others to report any signs of screwworm after the first cases appeared there in 2026. Joel Angel Juarez/Getty Images Although there have been only a couple of cases reported in wildlife, that isn’t necessarily reassuring. Wildlife are far more likely to carry the parasite without being detected. Once the screwworm is detected, treatment would also be much more complicated for wildlife than for livestock, because wildlife cannot be treated individually and thus are more dependent on the use of sterile flies to eradicate screwworm. For this reason, quickly identifying areas with New World screwworm and targeting those areas by releasing sterile flies would be more important than ever. Tapping an army of conservationists: Hunters Fortunately, there is an army of conservationists across the country who spend much of their time afield. These conservationists are also known as hunters. According to the latest U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service National Survey of Fishing, Hunting, and Wildlife-Associated Recreation, nearly 11.5 million hunters pursue big game and spend part of the fall and winter in the field hunting ungulate species such as deer and elk. Hunters can be the first line of defense in tracking screwworm infections in wildlife. Lovz2hike via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA White-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) hunters alone are expected to harvest about 6 million deer during the 2026-27 season and will observe millions more. Hunters also review tens of millions of wildlife pictures collected each year by game cameras used for scouting. That level of surveillance can’t be matched. New Mexico’s Department of Agriculture has already called on hunters to report any suspicious larvae, particularly in Grant and Otero counties, where screwworm has been found in livestock. Hunters of all kinds, everywhere, can help. What to watch for as a hunter If you’re a hunter, be on the lookout for wounded animals, especially those with visible maggots, and for unusual behaviors such as restlessness, lethargy, or biting or licking wounds. Do not move harvested animals from the field if they show signs of a New World screwworm infection. Doing so could further spread the parasite. Instead, contact the area’s state wildlife agency, the U.S. Department of Agriculture office or a local veterinarian immediately. As hunting seasons get underway across the country, an army of conservationists will be in the field, and they have an important role to play in detecting and managing screwworm’s spread. Hunters already contribute to conservation through license fees, excise taxes and keeping wildlife populations at healthy densities. In the face of New World screwworm, their observations may be most valuable for protecting livestock. This article, originally published Nov. 6, 2026, has been updated with a rising number of cases. 39929d6f6657fb23: Amazon Web Services (AWS) looks set to win more than a billion pounds of UK taxpayers' money under a new Home Office contract for public cloud hosting.

A planning notice, published on October 30, covers the renewal of the department's public cloud services, to meet its current and future hosting needs. The estimated value is £881,621,007 ($1.18 billion), which passes £1 billion once VAT is included.

AWS won the existing contract with the Home Office in 2023 for about £450 million (c $603 million). The Register has asked the Home Office why the figure has risen so much, and will update this article if it responds.

Once awarded, the contract is expected to run from December 2027 to December 2029, with a possible extension to December 2031 (four years in total). A market engagement event for suppliers on the G-Cloud 15 Lot 1A procurement framework is scheduled for December 8, giving bidders the chance to pitch.
The Home Office would not say who else is being considered, saying it does not comment on ongoing procurement.

The notice lands as digital sovereignty becomes a bigger problem in the UK and across Europe, amid suspicion that US authorities have cut off access to American technology for political reasons. A survey found that about three-quarters of businesses in the UK, France, and Germany fear Washington could abruptly sever access to the US tech platforms they rely on.
Earlier this year, the Open Rights Group warned politicians that the UK is far too dependent on US technology companies to run critical operations.

Whitehall is mindful of its over-reliance on American hyperscalers. As The Register revealed in 2024, the Cabinet Office admitted - in an internal document seen by us - that the government’s negotiating power had been inhibited by vendor lock-in.

It said the "UK government’s current approach to cloud adoption and management across its departments faces several challenges" which combined result "in risk concentration and vendor lock-in that inhibit UK government’s negotiating power over the cloud vendors." It acknowledged "the existing dominance of AWS and Azure in the UK Government’s cloud services is set to continue."

A source at one supplier that works with the public sector said the UK administration was "failing to support UK [cloud] providers, it says they can’t meet scale and that is garbage." They claimed that in many cases the government people writing the tenders are advised by professional services companies to favor the hyperscalers. The professional services companies are then "rewarded" as migration or integration partners, our source claimed.

The UK government also pledged to steer more business to small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) in an action plan published last month. In August it added smaller, local suppliers to G-Cloud 15, though a place on the framework does not guarantee any business.
Pledges like this are nothing new, and they have largely come to nothing, as we reported in 2005, 2013, 2016, and 2018.

According to public sector intelligence platform BidSkim, AWS takes 75 percent of the government money on cloud contracts, worth about £1.22 billion ($1.6 billion). It estimates that Microsoft Azure has more contracts, but these are smaller and add up to £355 million ($475 million), while Google Cloud is on £47 million ($63 million) and Oracle Cloud $15 million ($20 million).
The Reg has asked AWS to comment. ®

Even industries supposedly best placed to benefit from the technology have little to boast about. Productivity growth has improved in AI-heavy sectors such as information and communications, but has yet to exceed pre-pandemic averages.

That's not to say AI isn't doing anything for the British economy. The bank estimates that AI-related activity has accounted for just under a fifth of UK GDP growth since the beginning of 2026, though much of that appears to come from companies developing and deploying the technology rather than businesses becoming more productive by using it.

"The contribution to growth from AI to date appears to reflect activity in the upstream development and implementation of AI technologies rather than broader gains from their adoption elsewhere in the economy," the report said. In other words, selling AI is proving rather more lucrative than actually using it,

The bank also cautioned against giving AI too much credit for Britain's recent productivity improvements. Much of the increase appears to reflect businesses hiring fewer workers while output continues to grow, partly as companies unwind post-pandemic staffing decisions and respond to higher employment costs.

And despite predictions that AI will make vast swathes of the workforce redundant, firms responding to the Bank's Decision Maker Panel survey reported virtually no overall impact on employment so far. The technology is, however, making some employers less inclined to hire new staff or replace those who leave.

Other studies suggest businesses are still waiting for the payoff. A Gartner survey published last month found that while three-quarters of corporate board members expected AI to improve productivity and cut costs, just 3 percent of organizations had actually achieved their targets. Meanwhile, 38 percent were already over budget on AI spending, yet 85 percent planned to spend even more next year.

Another study involving nearly 6,000 executives, published in February, found that more than 80 percent of firms had seen no discernible impact from AI on either employment or productivity. Apparently, the answer to disappointing returns is to keep writing checks.

That growing disconnect between AI spending and actual returns has also caught the attention of financial watchdogs. The International Monetary Fund warned last month that the AI spending spree could come back to bite investors if the promised profits don't show up, potentially dragging the wider economy down with it.

The Bank for International Settlements sounded a similar alarm in June, comparing the current spending spree to the dotcom boom of the 1990s. Its concern is that tech giants are committing enormous sums to infrastructure on the assumption that AI will eventually deliver equally enormous returns, leaving them exposed if reality fails to cooperate.

However, AI is already making its presence felt in one area: prices. The Bank of England noted that surging demand for AI-related products, including memory chips, has pushed up export prices in China and other Asian economies, raising import costs for Britain.
So while businesses are still waiting for their AI-powered productivity windfall, the costs of the boom are already making their way through the economy.

The bank isn't writing off the technology just yet. Businesses surveyed expect AI to add around 0.9 percentage points to annual productivity growth over the next three years, with the gains split roughly equally between faster output growth and slower employment growth.
It seems the AI industry's most impressive productivity achievement is convincing businesses to keep opening their wallets. ®

c5841b2157571ae8: The UK government is paving the way for rules requiring essential service operators and digital providers to guard against losing control of AI agents and report incidents when safeguards fail.

An amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which is passing through Parliament, would give ministers powers to regulate the deployment and reporting of agentic AI in certain organizations. The new clause was introduced during the bill's third reading in the House of Lords this week.

In an explanatory note, ministers outlined plans for safeguards, notification of affected organizations, preservation of evidence, and government-led incident reviews. The measures would require consultation and parliamentary approval through secondary legislation.

The move follows a series of incidents. Last month, OpenAI revealed that its agents repeatedly strayed beyond their intended scope, prompting the company to notify more than 100 organizations about the issues. That came after July's incident, in which an OpenAI agent accessed the internet and breached machine learning platform Hugging Face. The episode, and the potential for more damage from poorly designed AI agent deployments, have prompted MPs to question whether UK law can deal with such threats.

Speaking to The Register, Stuart Davey, a partner at law firm Pinsent Masons, described the clause as "quite novel." Rather than directly imposing new duties, it would allow ministers to introduce rules and investigatory powers covering regulated organizations. Davey said that could include powers "to look where there has been such an AI agentic compromise or issue, and do some things... appoint inspectors, enter and search premises, seize and retain documents." Under the proposals, the minister could confer certain powers on regulators, requiring action from targeted organizations.

Potentially affected organizations include gas and electricity suppliers, managed service providers, and cloud providers deploying AI agents for customers. Foundation model developers would not automatically fall within scope simply because they build the underlying technology.

"Where there's a security or operational compromise in relation to a relevant network or information system, that would seem to capture those managed service providers or cloud computing providers who are using AI, and there's that loss of control," said Davey. He advised cloud and managed service providers to track whether the proposed measures become law.

Evin McMullen, CEO and co-founder of AI identity and control infrastructure company AmanTrue, said the amendment recognizes loss of oversight or control as a security risk but does not itself impose new duties.

"The amendment allows future regulations to introduce investigatory and enforcement powers where an incident involves an AI agent, targeting organizations running essential digital services," he said.

"The deployer of an AI agent chooses its permissions, connects it to systems, and gives it access to data. When something goes wrong, the deployer is the party that will be expected to explain what happened.

"Accountability stays with the organization that put the agent into the system, and ultimately with executives and the board. Whether model builders are captured will depend on how the regulations are written and whether a builder sits in a regulated category or a regulated supply chain." ®

996a31376cbe5e02: I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour.

I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round.

Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.

But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors.

With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there.

But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide.

The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing.

When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said.

Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.)

You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though. Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist. I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger.

In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet. That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle.

The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled. But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was. As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out.

Still, it’s not all slapstick and whimsy. If Tau Robotics or its competitors succeeds in training robots to clean autonomously and inexpensively, people could lose their livelihoods, and the United States is a long way away from implementing policies to take care of those left unemployed by AI.

But Weinzierl maintains that someday turning over cleaning work to robots could make a lot of sense. “Cleaning is not a job that a lot of people really actively want to be doing—there’s high turnover, there’s a high risk of injury,” she said when we spoke after the cleanings. “We need people, and we don’t have them, and no one wants to do it.” She said that the company is also starting to consider someday deploying the robots for other dangerous or physically challenging jobs, such as mold remediation and home health care.

Tau Robotics still has a long way to go: The amount of data needed to train robots to do the varied and complicated tasks of apartment cleaning is probably enormous, and the company has completed only a couple hundred cleanings so far. But it’s remarkable that there are now humanoid robots able to clean your toilets and mop your floors, even if they need quite a bit of human help to do so. The Jetsons no longer feels quite so far away.
7117a84a7ab3afa6: NHS England CEO Sir Jim Mackey plans to tell Palantir to clear future claims about its Federated Data Platform's benefits with his team – although he admits that could be difficult to enforce.

Speaking to the Health and Social Care Committee this week, Labour MP Ben Coleman noted that NHS England had cautioned against attributing improvements directly to the platform, but said newly appointed Palantir UK senior vice president Tom Watson "is making claims that [Palantir] is making a difference, and that it's due to Palantir that changes are taking place."
Responding, Mackey said he would write to Palantir and "tell them that they have to share with us and clear with us any benefits claimed in the future."
But getting Palantir to comply could be another matter. "They should share them with us, but contractually, it looks hard to enforce," Mackey said.

The planned letter follows repeated questions about the evidence NHS England and Palantir have used to promote the Federated Data Platform (FDP). NHS England awarded the £330 million contract to a Palantir-led consortium in November 2023 to help improve planning and efficiency.

In July, campaign group Foxglove wrote to the UK health minister questioning figures used in Parliament to justify the contract. The Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) also began examining the evidence.

NHS England had said that as of June, 139 trusts used the platform, with 137 reporting benefits. It said an Inpatient Care Coordination Solution tool based on the FDP had helped hospitals perform procedures on an additional 111,589 patients. However, a Freedom of Information request later found that nearly a third of NHS trusts using Palantir's health data platform were performing fewer patient procedures than before it went live.
Later that month, the OSR said NHS England had accepted that it needed to communicate its claims about FDP performance more clearly.
The regulator noted that NHS England had published on its website a caveat saying that it could not "draw conclusions about cause and effect as other variables have not been controlled for."

Last month, Watson, the former deputy leader of the Labour Party, sought to rebut what he described as misinformation about the FDP, repeating the statement that 137 trusts were already reporting benefits without mentioning the caveats.

In a statement on X, Watson said the OSR had pointed out that there had not yet been a study on the FDP that controls for other factors like staffing level changes or industrial action. "That's a fair note of caution."

In a prepared video, he said Northampton General Hospital, University Hospitals of Derby and Burton, and Chelsea and Westminster Hospital had all produced figures showing they are benefiting from using the platform.
"Can we prove that every one of those procedures happened because of our software? No. But does that mean we should ignore what the hospitals are telling us? Of course not," he said.

5f6e3d9db66e4bc1: Britain's ambitions for AI, advanced chips, and clean energy rest on mineral supply chains dominated by China, and MPs say they cannot establish whether ministers have a credible plan to reduce that dependence.

The House of Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee has set ministers ten tests for securing critical minerals. Its verdict is hardly glowing – it cannot be confident the government passes any of them.

The tests cover whether ministers know which industries and technologies need protecting, what minerals they require, where supplies could be disrupted, and how domestic production, overseas partnerships, skills, and financing will close the gaps.

In a report published today, the committee warns that diversifying supplies will take ten to 15 years, and will require sustained investment and cooperation with allies. Completely cutting China out is neither realistic nor desirable, it says. Leaving Beijing with so much leverage is another matter.

Critical minerals underpin everything from batteries and semiconductors to datacenters and military equipment. The designation reflects their economic or security importance and vulnerability to supply disruption, rather than membership of an especially exclusive geological club.

The UK – like pretty much all major industrialized economies including the US, the EU, Japan, and India – is almost entirely dependent on imports of these materials and mineral products. But digging up more ore outside China would solve only part of the problem. The bigger bottleneck is processing.

Citing International Energy Agency figures, the committee says China is the leading refiner for 19 of 20 strategic minerals, with an average market share of 70 percent. A different flag over the mine does not necessarily mean a different route through the refinery.

The exposure extends beyond chips and batteries. As The Register reported in August, erbium is used to amplify signals in fiber-optic links, while yttrium goes into components including ceramic capacitors. IEEE Spectrum warned that China effectively monopolized the processing of both into the industrially usable materials manufacturers need.

That concentration has already caused disruption. China's rare earth export controls in April 2025, introduced following US tariffs, rippled through manufacturing supply chains and forced temporary automotive plant closures. British manufacturers can suffer even when Britain isn't the intended target.

The committee also highlights gallium and germanium, used in advanced semiconductors for radar, communications, and electronic warfare. China accounts for 95 percent and 93 percent of their global production respectively, according to the report [PDF].

Beijing flexing its leverage over chip materials is not new. China announced export licensing requirements for gallium and germanium in July 2023 amid tightening Western restrictions on semiconductor technology.

Yet MPs say the government has not clearly identified which domestic industrial and technological capabilities it wants to protect, making it difficult to determine which supply chains deserve priority.

Nor do import statistics reveal the whole exposure. Minerals can arrive inside batteries, magnets, and other manufactured components, disappearing from view as individual materials. Businesses themselves may not know precisely what lies several layers down their supply chains.

The committee wants confidential mapping and stress-testing with firms in critical sectors, followed by joint purchasing arrangements with allies to give new mining and refining projects dependable customers.

Committee chair Liam Byrne said: "Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy. We cannot re-arm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.

"Yet sixteen years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed. We don't know enough about what minerals we need or where to find them. Our energy costs make processing uneconomic, we're exporting valuable metal waste, and our public finance institutions are shackled by outdated rules."
More than a shopping list

The committee's five-part prescription is to identify the capabilities Britain must protect, map their mineral needs, expand domestic mining, processing, and recycling, pool purchasing power with allies, and establish a dedicated financing facility.
The proposed facility would bring together public funding bodies to back projects through grants, equity, loans, guarantees, and long-term purchase agreements.
"We're never going to eliminate Chinese minerals from our supply chains. But it's foolish to leave Britain exposed to economic coercion when we could be building alternative supplies," Byrne said.
"That's why we need a new Critical Minerals Finance Facility with the financial firepower to invest in new mines, processing plants and recycling, working with our allies to share the costs."

The report argues that existing institutions leave gaps, particularly for early-stage projects. It recommends expanding UK Export Finance's remit and allowing British International Investment to take equity stakes in overseas mineral projects.
Long-term purchasing commitments and price guarantees could help keep strategically important projects commercially viable despite volatile mineral prices.

There is also material closer to home. The report says 80 percent of UK metal products classified as waste are exported. MPs want better sorting and separation infrastructure, alongside more detailed trade data to establish exactly what valuable scrap is leaving the country.
For domestic projects, they recommend designated critical mineral clusters with permitting deadlines, help navigating approvals, energy support, and priority grid access.

Stockpiles could provide a short-term buffer too. The committee calls for an initial reserve covering approximately 60 days of minerals needed for defense capabilities, while stressing that warehouses are no substitute for diversified supply.

None of this offers a quick escape from dependence on China. The committee's argument is that Britain needs to decide what it must protect, work out what those industries actually consume, and help finance alternatives before the next disruption.

"De-risking even a prudent proportion of our supplies will take over a decade. Britain cannot afford to drift," Byrne said. "We must act now before dangerous dependencies become strategic liabilities." ®

f48959b9713d2dd2: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 6 — Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) has put in place regulatory requirements for financial institutions to maintain adequate cybersecurity safeguards, continuously strengthening their defences, said Governor Datuk Seri Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour.

The governor stressed that cybersecurity has always been a priority because it is the foundation of confidence and it could have implications for financial stability.

“We expect financial institutions to adopt a proactive and comprehensive approach to cybersecurity, with strong measures to prevent cyber incidents (as well as) detect and contain threats promptly,” he told Bernama.

Abdul Rasheed said BNM continuously reviews and updates the guidelines, regulations, requirements and standards to ensure that financial institutions remain equipped to address emerging cyber threats.

Incident reporting arrangements and platforms are also in place to enable the central bank and financial institutions to exchange threat intelligence. This helps identify emerging threats early and reduces the risk of contagion across the financial sector.
He noted that BNM’s Risk Management in Technology (RMiT) policy document requires financial institutions to conduct annual “cyber drills”.
These exercises are intended to test banks’ systems, identify weaknesses and ensure they can maintain operational resilience even if their systems are compromised.
He said cybersecurity preparedness must extend across all financial institutions, regardless of their size, as weaknesses in one institution could potentially expose the wider financial system.
“In cybersecurity, the weakest link would affect everyone as entities within the system are all interconnected. Even a small bank could pose a risk to the entire financial system,” he said.

In the event of an attack, the immediate priority would be to contain the threat by isolating affected systems, disconnecting connections where necessary and conducting checks to minimise contagion risk to other systems or institutions.
He said affected institutions might have to temporarily suspend certain online operations while investigations and security assessments are carried out before services could safely resume.
He added that BNM expects financial institutions to recover operations with minimal disruption while safeguarding customer information. — Bernama

0b3108282dcb5b70: The autofill feature of Apple's Safari browser appears to be suffering from a date handling error that occasionally leads it to supply an incorrect credit card expiration date when filling out forms.

The supposed issue has been a sore spot for Apple customers dating back at least to 2017, when the author of an Apple Community forum post complained about changes to the month field in the Autofill credit card expiration date when moving between time zones.

"I've noticed for the last year or so, whenever I travel from Eastern time zone (my home) to Central time zone or even Pacific time zone that my credit card expiration date month changes in Safari Autofill," the Safari user wrote.
Another post in 2021 raised similar concerns.

"I don't know how to reproduce this," the author wrote. "Every few months Safari on any of my devices changes the expiration month of all of my stored credit cards by decreasing the month by 1, for example instead of 10/2029 it changes it to 09/2029."
Three years later, another person posting to Apple's Community forum reported the same issue.

"For a few years now every time I use Autofill on my computer my credit cards (ALL of them) always have their expiration dates change one month earlier," the 2024 post says. "I thought it was just a glitch on my computer but I bought a new computer and didn't transfer anything from my old one and it is still doing it."
An unrelated Autofill bug report from 2024 suggests that if there is an issue, it resides in Apple-owned Safari code rather than Safari's open source WebKit engine.

Wherever the bug may reside, Safari's unreliable handling of credit card dates has kept a complaint-filled Reddit thread going for four years. And the reported month-shifting has been noted in other threads, too.
The Register was unable to reproduce the described behavior, but a reader insists it's still a problem.
"The Safari AutoFill feature sometimes fills in the credit card expiration date wrong," the reader explained. "My credit card expires in December, but sometimes Apple helpfully enters November."
"To be clear, the card is stored correctly when inspected in Settings," our tipster added. "The off-by-one error only happens when filling out a form in Safari, and not consistently."

One possible way this might happen is if the Safari Autofill code implemented the expiration date using Swift's DateComponent type and stored it as a Calendar object with UTC as the TimeZone identifier. Doing so would anchor the date to a specific time. If the date components were extracted in Pacific Time, the value would be represented as eight hours ahead (PST). So 9/1/2027 at 00:00 would appear as 8/31/2027 at 16:00.

Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but we're told Apple's Help Desk – or "Helpless Desk" as our source put it – advised clearing the browser cache and re-entering details of the affected credit card.
If that works, it suggests Safari's handling of cached data in the context of Autofill dates may need to be revisited.
Apple does not maintain a public bug database and the community-maintained OpenRadar sheds no light on these reports. ®

70838a2d72ac3386: Welcome to Friday and therefore to a fresh edition of On Call, The Register's weekly tale of tech support trials and tribulations that readers kindly share.
This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Mason," who told us he once worked at a hospital doing tech support for its research labs.
"One of the labs was for a doctor who was one of the world's top organ transplant researchers" Mason told On Call.
The doctor was also a voracious consumer of – ahem – adult entertainment, a habit that saw his PC and other machines around the lab often come down with a nasty case of malware.
Mason got to clean that up, sometimes multiple times in a single week.
The doctor's foibles were widely known around the hospital, as was the fact that his activities violated several workplace policies.
Mason pointed this out to his boss every time he cleaned up a fresh malware outbreak but such was the doctor's status that management never intervened.

And then the hospital was hit by a nasty cyber-worm that did a lot of damage. During the cleanup, Mason's colleagues found logs that showed the doctor's PC was the source of the infection, and that he had been indulging in his online hobby at the time the worm arrived.
Mason assumed this would be the moment at which the doctor would finally be held accountable and face disciplinary action.

Instead the doctor made a bargain with the IT department to henceforth use only a designated PC when pursuing – ahem – personal and/or intimate matters. And he would only use office PCs for actual work.
The hospital's tech team rescued a PC from its e-waste pile for this job.
"Get this thing going and deliver it to Doctor Pervert," Mason's boss ordered.

By this stage, Mason had had enough. He escalated his protests, telling his boss that indulging this doctor was unprofessional, likely exposed the hospital to lawsuits, wasted IT department resources, and was just wrong.
"What do you want to hear?" his boss replied. "The CIO told me do this or get another job."
After Mason prepped that PC, he only needed to clean up malware about once a year – after the poor machine was so overrun with malware that it no longer served the doctor's purposes.
Mason left the hospital while this PC was still in place.

"You'll be shocked, no doubt, to learn that years later the doctor's graduate students filed a lawsuit," he told On Call. "And that the separate fun-time computer was one of the pieces of evidence that the hospital knew about his – ahem – proclivities and not just ignored them but facilitated them."

Have you been asked to cover up revolting behavior? Or ignore policy? Click here to share your story with On Call. It's our policy to tell a great tech support story week, so we appreciate every contribution. ®
